articles.title: Bukele deploys thousands of soldiers to Haiti
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: El Salvador’s right-wing president, Nayib Bukele, announced on October 29, that he will deploy a military force of nearly 2,000 soldiers to Haiti. The Salvadoran president has justified the measure by citing the disappearance of four Salvadoran soldiers on October 18. The Salvadoran soldiers reportedly went missing following an armed attack in Croix-des-Bouquets, near the capital Port-au-Prince, involving the armored vehicle in which they were traveling. According to some reports , the attackers used very powerful weapons and explosives. Since then, the whereabouts of the soldiers remain unknown, and it is unclear whether they are still alive. According to Bukele, thousands of Salvadoran soldiers are conducting search operations. Several critics have claimed that the deployment amounts to a military invasion of Haiti. Bukele and unelected Haitian prime minister justify deployment The Salvadoran president has denied accusations of an invasion: “This is not an operation against the Haitian people, nor is it an invasion of Haiti. We are not a major power. We have no interest in coming to dominate the Haitian people, nor in laying our hands on Haiti’s wealth … All we want is for our four aviation technicians to return home.” In announcing the deployment, Bukele also addressed the issue of who is funding the operation: “We are practically the only ones paying for this operation. Although we receive a little logistical assistance from some other countries, it is with our own modest budget that we are covering 90% of the expenses.” Furthermore, Bukele justified , in a biblical tone, the presence of his soldiers by stating that El Salvador also knows the hardships of gang violence: “We have gone through the same suffering that Haiti is going through today. We have experienced a bloodbath that was even more terrible than what the Haitian people are suffering now … We are not coming to Haiti to make money, because no one is paying us for this. We’ve come to Haiti to fight the bad guys. But this is what I ask of you: Trust us, pray to the one true God, and ask Him to heal Haiti.” For his part, de facto Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé stated in a press release that the deployment of thousands of Salvadoran soldiers is not an invasion, but rather an operation of “bilateral and cooperative coordination” to locate the missing soldiers. Critics denounce deployment as further destabilization of Haiti Human rights advocates, on the other hand, have warned against foreign interventions that historically have further destabilized Haiti and increased violence. One of the countries in the region most closely aligned with the US, and a key part of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” bloc, El Salvador’s deployment is seen as far more than just a small regional nation’s military involvement. Donald Trump himself reportedly gave the Salvadoran president the green light for military action. Further, Bukele’s own comparison to gang violence in El Salvador draws attention to the various groups and communities that have denounced his iron-grip response in the country. Many say the pretext of gang violence was used to institute an ongoing state of emergency that stripped basic democratic rights and led to a systematic consolidation of power by Bukele’s loyalists. Investigative journalists at El Faro also exposed that Bukele made a secret pact with the gangs before implementing his iron-grip model. The suggestion that a similar approach needs to be taken in Haiti is exactly what human rights activists have been sounding the alarm about. But understanding the implications of El Salvador’s deployment requires looking beyond the immediate search for the missing soldiers. Haiti’s security crisis is inseparable from the political instability, foreign interference, and historical structures of domination that have shaped the country for generations. Political destabilization or gang problem? The four Salvadoran soldiers in Haiti were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a UN-authorized military deployment of personnel from different countries allegedly to help control the security situation in the country. The GSF has come under heavy criticism as the latest iteration of the UN occupation of Haiti which has already caused immense harm to the Haitian people and has been incapable of “controlling” the situation of violence. In Haiti, public trust in the transitional leadership is already low. High-ranking officials, including former National Police Chief Frantz Elbé, faced widespread public backlash and demands for removal following allegations of political corruption, failure to protect citizens, and covert ties between elements of his police force and local gangs. Citing this corruption, experts say the situation in Haiti is much deeper than a gang crisis. “These gangs regularly receive weapons and ammunition from the United States,” says Venezuelan academic Guillermo Barreto. “This action indicates a project that seeks to make the functioning of a nation unviable. But this attack on the Haitian nation is not recent. Haiti has been under siege by imperial powers since its independence. “

articles.title: Half a million join youth-led protests in France
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Saturday, October 31, opened as another day of mass mobilizations across France. For almost two months – led by high school and university student demands for stronger public education – hundreds of thousands of people have been joining demonstrations against the policies of President Emmanuel Macron and successive administrations. According to student unions , at least 500,000 people joined the demonstrations on Saturday, including 200,000 in the capital. “We are now in the sixth week of mobilization by high school students and, more broadly, the youth,” Christophe Benoît, deputy general secretary of the General Confederation of Labor (Confédération Générale du Travail, CGT) in Lille, told BreakThrough News . “It’s a movement best summed up in the words of a high school student speaking at a recent assembly: ‘We see the social hardship of our parents and we see our own future reflected in it.'” Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education Students and youth have tabled demands to strengthen the public education system in France. These include investment in school infrastructure, ending the course selection platform Parcoursup, and ensuring fair and equitable access to higher education. Their demands are clearly linked to grievances raised by other groups during Macron’s presidency, which have warned against the devastating impact of raising the retirement age , eroding workplace rights, and leaving the cost-of-living crisis unchecked. “Against the politics of Macron” Speaking from the demonstration in Paris on Saturday, Maurizio Coppola from the International Peoples’ Assembly (IPA) emphasized the protests are taking place “against the austerity measures, against the politics of Macron.” Over the past ten years, Coppola added, these policies have been “dismantling salaries and social services.” Student protests have maintained a decisively anti-fascist character. Source: Jean-Luc Mélenchon/Facebook The convergence of the youth and student movement with trade unions and groups like the gilets jaunes , the Yellow Vests, has deeply shaken Macron’s and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s position. Faced with a general mobilization based on clearly progressive demands, authorities responded with violence , with dozens of injuries and thousands of student arrests reported since the protests began. An authoritarian turn in France? The state’s response has been so openly violent as to raise serious concern among human rights organizations. Amnesty International France contextualized parts of this response as part of a possible authoritarian turn by the country’s authorities. “A state that adopts authoritarian practices seeks to silence dissenting voices by restricting space for expression,” they wrote. “In France today, the right to demonstrate is under serious attack, with a series of protest bans, arrests and police repression.” The government has also attempted to discourage participation in the mobilizations by promoting and imposing protest bans and restrictions. Among other things, the route of Paris’ Saturday march was contested in court until the very last minute. High school and university students have been demanding more investment into public education. Source: Union étudiante/Facebook While labor and student unions pushed for a march in central Paris, the city’s police administration insisted on moving it to a more distant zone. Organizers contested this imposition in court, warning that the decision not only threatened to create chaos but also represented a notable attack on the right to protest. Even though the courts ruled in favor of the organizers, the Council of State – a body that acts as the highest administrative court and advisor to the government – overruled this decision and forced last-minute changes. Protesters in Paris joined the demonstration anyway, just as thousands of people took to the streets in other cities. General strike on November 5 The success of the movement continues to encourage new mobilizations, including, notably, a general strike on November 5. “It’s a general strike against Macron, against his system, against the war economy he has implemented,” Coppola said. “This solidarity cannot be stopped by some small measures, this solidarity cannot be stopped by the repression the French state is applying to the movement.” “We are dealing with questions of what kind of society we want,” Benoît emphasized, referring to the general strike. “It’s absolutely essential that the labor movement join forces with the youth to win real progress – for the entire population, too – against the capitalist policies we’ve been suffering from in France for decades now.” “We need a movement, a general movement, and we need to hit those who are really making the decisions in this country, that is to say, the employers.” By last Thursday, the CGT alone had already noted 185 industrial action announcements ahead of November 5. Student unions announced additional actions in the coming week – including a call to occupy high schools and universities – to support the general strike and protest demands.
